A build-along course

Building Sequent

An exchange. Orders match by price and time, the opening auction clears everything at one price, every trade posts to a ledger that balances by construction, and the entire venue can be replayed from its log and arrive at exactly the same state. Built from an empty folder, with every bug found along the way written down.

Everything we'll cover

  1. 01 What we are building A stock exchange: an order book, an opening auction, pre-trade risk, central clearing and a double-entry ledger — with an event log the whole thing can be rebuilt from.
  2. 02 The four hard parts Ordering, money, reconstructability and blast radius. Each one dictates a design decision we make before writing any code.
  3. 03 The workspace Six packages, and a dependency rule that makes the most important property of the engine impossible to break by accident.
  4. 04 Money, as integers Scaled integers, branded types, and a `parsePrice` that never multiplies by 10,000.
  5. 05 Ids that explain themselves Deterministic identifiers derived from the sequence number, and why a UUID would make replay impossible.
  6. 06 The vocabulary: commands and events Two discriminated unions, validated with valibot, versioned from the first line.
  7. 07 The order book Price-time priority, a binary search, and why the depth bar is a `scaleX` rather than a width.
  8. 08 `apply` as a pure function One function, `(state, command) → events`, with no clock, no database and no randomness. Everything else in the venue is a consequence of it.
  9. 09 Pre-trade risk Nine checks in a deliberate order, a fat-finger collar, and a kill switch that stops a firm dead.
  10. 10 Self-trade prevention Stopping a firm trading with itself — and the bug where the fix threw away fills it had already applied.
  11. 11 The opening auction Finding the one price that trades the most, four tie-breaks deep — and the bug where multi-trade auctions dropped fills.
  12. 12 A table as a log Two append-only tables, enforced by triggers, and why SQLite is a defensible choice for the spine of an exchange.
  13. 13 The sequencer One writer, a cached high-water mark, and a check that catches the botched deploy where two engines are running.
  14. 14 Checkpoints, and the transaction that makes them safe How a consumer remembers where it got to, and the one rule that makes a crash survivable.
  15. 15 Snapshots, and the promise they must not break Making restart fast without letting the venue depend on a cache — and the fault-injection test that caught it depending on one.
  16. 16 The engine process The loop, one transaction per command, graceful shutdown — and the file-descriptor leak that killed it after ten thousand orders.
  17. 17 Projections are caches Turning events into queryable tables, and the discipline that lets you delete all of them.
  18. 18 Double entry, and the constraint that makes it work Every transaction sums to zero, signed amounts instead of two columns, and corrections that are entries rather than edits.
  19. 19 Multi-tenancy and authorisation Five roles, thirteen actions, and a pure function small enough to enumerate every input of.
  20. 20 Keys, secrets, and what may be stored in clear scrypt, timing-safe comparison, two-part keys — and the one secret that must not be hashed.
  21. 21 The gateway The only way a command reaches the log — and the one line that stops a client trading as somebody else.
  22. 22 A Kit 3 app from nothing No svelte.config.js, no $lib, and a tsconfig that has to say which files are yours.
  23. 23 Environment variables, declared src/env.ts replaces the four $env modules, and makes leaking a secret into the browser a type error.
  24. 24 Remote functions query, command, form and query.live — and why every argument needs a schema even though the caller is your own page.
  25. 25 Sessions and cookies Signing in without a library, and the two details that stop it leaking information.
  26. 26 The CSRF check we wrote ourselves Kit 3 blocked a legitimate DELETE and allowed a cross-origin JSON POST. Here is the bug, and the replacement.
  27. 27 Async Svelte, and the getter trap await inside $derived is wonderful, and it has one ordering rule that will cost you an afternoon if you do not know it.
  28. 28 A public API worth using One error shape, a request id on every response, and the four bugs that curl found in an afternoon.
  29. 29 API keys Two-part keys, shown once, and why the prefix is not decoration.
  30. 30 Rate limits and pagination A token bucket with no timers, and cursors that do not silently drop rows when the tape moves.
  31. 31 The transactional outbox The dual-write problem, which has exactly one solution, and the worker that drains it.
  32. 32 Webhooks that cannot be forged HMAC signatures with a timestamp, and the SSRF check that let the cloud metadata service through.
  33. 33 Mobile first, for real Designing a trading terminal for a 390px phone first — and the flex default that gives half the web a horizontal scrollbar.
  34. 34 Tables that are measurements Why restacking a table into cards destroys it, and the sticky-position overflow bug that took a browser to find.
  35. 35 Motion that means something A motion system whose defining feature is how little of it there is — and the reveal that made the app unusable for 800ms.
  36. 36 The depth ladder The one component with a real performance problem — and why the obvious optimisation solves the wrong half of it.
  37. 37 Live screens, and the stale phase The bug where a refresh returned the old answer — and why the fix was to stop refreshing.
  38. 38 Migrations without a framework Sixty lines that apply a change once and record it — and the three rules that make a rolling deploy survivable.
  39. 39 Feature flags, and the pause A flag may change what the venue offers. It may never change what the engine decides.
  40. 40 Billing from the log No payment provider — because everything that goes wrong with billing goes wrong before the charge.
  41. 41 Tests that find real bugs Property-based, fault injection, load — and an honest account of which kinds actually caught something.
  42. 42 Running it Four numbers worth watching at 3am, a health check that knows the difference between slow and broken, and where to go next.

Every chapter shows the real code from the finished project in sequent. Type it out rather than pasting where you can — the errors you make and fix are the part that sticks. Roughly a dozen chapters end with a bug that was genuinely in this codebase, and how it was found.
